How to estimate a car's future resale value

Begin with a current private-party market value, not the original MSRP or the amount still owed. Choose Annual depreciation rate to project forward from an assumed compound rate. Choose Known future resale value when you already have a residual estimate, lease-end value, guaranteed future value, or defensible future comparable and want to calculate the equivalent annual depreciation rate. Both modes produce a year-by-year value schedule, sale-cost estimate, future loan equity, and mileage context.

future resale value = current value x (1 - annual depreciation rate)^years

equivalent annual depreciation rate = 1 - (future value / current value)^(1 / years)

estimated net proceeds = resale value - selling costs - future loan payoff

Car resale value example

A car worth $28,000 today and depreciating 14% per year for three years has a modeled resale value of about $17,809.57. That means it retains about 63.6% of its current value and loses about $10,190.43. If selling costs equal 2% of the future value and the lender payoff at sale is $8,000, estimated net proceeds are about $9,453.38. Starting at 36,000 miles and driving 12,000 miles per year produces a projected odometer of 72,000 miles.

Calculate the depreciation rate from a known resale value

Reverse mode is useful when the future value is the known assumption. For example, a decline from $28,000 to $17,810 over three years corresponds to an annual compound depreciation rate of about 14%. The derived rate is not a market forecast; it is the single constant rate that mathematically connects the two values. It helps compare residual assumptions that cover different ownership periods.

A target above the current value is not accepted because this tool models depreciation rather than appreciation. Collectible, scarce, or unusually appreciating vehicles require a market-based valuation approach.

Use a defensible current market value

The starting value has more influence than any formatting choice in the calculator. Match year, make, model, trim, engine, drivetrain, options, title history, mileage, condition, and ZIP-code market. Review several local comparables and at least one recognized valuation source. Asking prices are evidence of seller expectations, not proof of completed transaction prices. This calculator has no VIN, auction, dealer inventory, or live transaction feed.

Kelley Blue Book's valuation documentation identifies actual condition, popularity, warranty, mileage, and local market factors as inputs that can affect vehicle value. Use the same valuation channel for both your baseline and later comparison; dealer retail, private-party, and trade-in figures are not interchangeable.

How mileage affects the result

Current and annual mileage are shown so you can test whether the future odometer is plausible and calculate modeled depreciation per added mile. Mileage does not independently change the formula because a universal dollar-per-mile adjustment would create false precision across different vehicles. Instead, reflect expected high or low mileage in the annual depreciation rate or known future value, using comparables with similar projected mileage.

projected odometer = current odometer + annual miles x years until sale

Condition, accident history, and maintenance

Mechanical condition, warning lights, tires, glass, paint, interior wear, odors, accident and title history, maintenance records, and required reconditioning can move an actual offer. A well-documented vehicle may be easier to sell, but maintenance spending does not automatically add the same amount to resale value. Re-estimate the current market value after a major accident, material damage, or a meaningful market change rather than relying on an old baseline.

Loan payoff, positive equity, and negative equity

Enter the expected lender payoff at the future sale date, not today's statement balance and not the sum of remaining scheduled payments. A payoff quote can include accrued interest and fees and may differ from the balance shown on a statement. Positive net proceeds mean the modeled sale value, after entered selling costs, exceeds the payoff. A negative result means additional money may be needed to release the lien.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's auto-loan terms define negative equity as owing more than the vehicle is worth. Its guidance recommends obtaining the payoff amount and researching the vehicle's approximate market value before deciding whether to sell or trade.

What to include as selling costs

Selling costs are modeled as a percentage of projected value. They can represent detailing, inspection, listing, consignment, transaction, document, or auction costs when those items apply. Set the rate to zero for a direct sale with no modeled costs. Do not include the loan payoff in the percentage because it is already deducted separately.

Compare slower and faster depreciation

The scenario table changes only the annual depreciation rate by the selected number of percentage points. With a 14% base rate and a 3-point range, the calculator compares 11%, 14%, and 17%. Current value, ownership period, selling-cost rate, payoff, and mileage stay fixed. This is a sensitivity test, not a confidence interval or probability forecast.

Resale value, depreciation, trade-in, and used-car value

This calculator answers a future private-sale planning question. Use the car depreciation calculator to compare constant and two-stage value-loss models with a residual floor. Use the used car value calculator to estimate current retail, private-party, and trade-in ranges from a local comparable. Use the trade-in value calculator to compare dealer offers, payoff equity, possible tax credit, and replacement financing.

How to improve your resale estimate

  1. Refresh the current market value with local, closely matched vehicles.
  2. Use an ownership period that matches your actual planned sale date.
  3. Project the odometer from realistic annual mileage.
  4. Test at least one slower and one faster depreciation scenario.
  5. Request a future payoff estimate from the lender rather than guessing from today's balance.
  6. Recalculate when mileage, condition, accident history, market demand, or the planned sale date changes.

Frequently asked questions

Is the projected resale value guaranteed?

No. It is a scenario based on entered values and a constant compound rate. Obtain current appraisals and offers when you are ready to sell.

What if net proceeds are negative?

The modeled payoff and selling costs exceed the projected sale value. That indicates possible negative equity under the assumptions.

Does annual mileage automatically reduce the value?

No. Mileage is reported as context because different models and markets respond differently. Reflect expected mileage through a defensible future value or rate.

Should I enter trade-in value as the starting value?

Use a current private-party value when estimating future private-sale proceeds. Use values from the same selling channel throughout the comparison.

Can the calculator model appreciation?

No. It accepts future values up to the current value and depreciation rates from 0% to less than 100%.
